title: Egypt, Greece and Rome
bigQuestion: How did ancient healers around the Mediterranean try to understand the body, and which of their ideas lasted?

story.title: The Scribe and the Broken Jaw
story.kicker: In ancient Egypt, a scribe copies careful steps for helping a patient with a broken jaw.
paragraphs: Imagine a quiet room in Egypt about 3,600 years ago. A scribe sits cross-legged with a roll of papyrus across his knees. He dips a reed pen in black ink. Next to him lies an older roll, cracked and faded. His job is to copy it word for word, so the knowledge will not be lost.

The old roll is about injuries. Each case starts with a title, like a broken jaw or a wound in the head. Then it tells the healer what to look for. Feel the jaw with your fingers. Check whether the bone moves. Look at the patient's face and ask what hurts.

The scribe switches to red ink for the headings, as Egyptian scribes often did. He writes the next part carefully. The healer should make a judgment: can this injury be treated, can it be tried, or is it beyond help? Then come the steps for care, such as bandages and rest.

The scribe does not know it, but part of a roll like this will survive. Today historians call it the Edwin Smith Papyrus. It shows that some ancient healers looked closely at the body, named what they saw and wrote it down in order. That habit is one root of medicine.
story.think: Why might it matter that the healer sorted each injury into treatable, worth trying, or not treatable before starting care?

lessons.title: The Edwin Smith Papyrus
lessons.mainIdea: The Edwin Smith Papyrus, from about 1600 BCE, describes injuries case by case, using careful looking and touching.
reading: In 1862 an American collector named Edwin Smith bought an old roll of *papyrus* in Luxor, Egypt. Papyrus is a paper-like material made from a river reed. The roll was about 1600 BCE, but experts think it was copied from an even older text. It is now one of the oldest known writings about surgery and injuries.

The papyrus describes 48 *cases*. A case is one patient's problem, written up with its signs and care. The cases start at the head and move down toward the chest and spine. For each one, the writer explains how to examine the patient: look, feel with the fingers, and ask questions.

The scholar James Henry Breasted of the University of Chicago published an English translation in 1930. Readers were struck by how practical the text is. Most cases use splints, bandages, stitches and rest, with only a little use of spells. It shows ancient Egyptian healers building knowledge by watching patients closely.

words.d: a paper-like writing material made in ancient Egypt from a river reed
one patient's problem, described with its signs, examination and care

look.title: A Case About a Broken Jaw
look.text: If you examine a man with a broken jaw, place your hand on it. If you find the break moving under your fingers, say: this is an injury I will try to treat.
look.cite: Edwin Smith Papyrus, about 1600 BCE, following the English translation by James Henry Breasted, 1930
look.prompt: Which words show the healer using the senses to examine the patient?

check.q: About when was the Edwin Smith Papyrus written?
check.why: The papyrus dates to about 1600 BCE. Edwin Smith bought it in 1862.

check.q: How are the 48 cases in the papyrus arranged?
choices: From the head moving down the body
check.why: The cases begin at the head and move down toward the chest and spine.

check.q: What kinds of care does the papyrus mostly describe?
check.why: The reading says most cases use practical care, with only a little use of spells.

lessons.title: The Ebers Papyrus
lessons.mainIdea: The Ebers Papyrus, from about 1550 BCE, collects hundreds of remedies and mixes practical care with spells.
reading: Another famous roll is named for Georg Ebers, a German scholar who bought it in 1873. The *Ebers Papyrus* dates to about 1550 BCE. It is much longer than the Edwin Smith roll. It holds around 700 remedies and many short passages about illness.

A *remedy* is something used to treat an illness. The Ebers remedies use honey, plants, minerals and animal products. Some use honey on wounds. Honey can slow the growth of some germs, so this idea has some support today. Many other remedies have no scientific support.

The Ebers Papyrus also includes spells and prayers. To Egyptian healers, medicine and religion worked together. The roll also describes the heart as a center with vessels running through the body. That idea was not fully correct, but it shows healers trying to explain how the body is connected.

words.d: an Egyptian medical roll from about 1550 BCE with hundreds of remedies
something used to treat an illness or injury

look.title: How Old Are These Writings?
look.cite: Dates commonly given by historians; see J. F. Nunn, Ancient Egyptian Medicine, 1996, and Roy Porter, The Greatest Benefit to Mankind, 1997
look.prompt: About how many years older are the Egyptian rolls than the Hippocratic writings? What might Greek healers have learned from Egypt?

check.q: What is the Ebers Papyrus mostly a collection of?
choices: Injury cases from head to spine
check.why: The Ebers Papyrus holds around 700 remedies and many passages about illness.

check.q: Which Ebers remedy has some support from science today?
check.why: Honey can slow the growth of some germs, so honey on wounds has some support.

check.q: How did Egyptian healers see medicine and religion?
check.why: The roll includes spells and prayers because medicine and religion worked together for them.

lessons.title: What Egypt Passed On
lessons.mainIdea: Egypt's written, organized approach to injuries and remedies influenced later healers around the Mediterranean.
reading: Egypt was famous in the ancient world for its doctors. The Greek writer Herodotus, about 440 BCE, said that Egyptian healers each focused on one part of the body. Historians are not sure how exact his report was. Still, it shows that others admired Egyptian medicine.

One lasting habit was careful *observation*. Observation means watching and noting what you see, hear and feel. The Edwin Smith cases ask the healer to examine first and decide second. Modern doctors do the same when they check a patient before choosing a treatment.

Another habit was the *prognosis*. A prognosis is a prediction about how an illness or injury will turn out. The Egyptian healer sorted injuries into those to treat, those to try, and those beyond help. Doctors today still think about the likely outcome before they plan care.

words.d: carefully watching and noting what you see, hear or feel
a prediction about how an illness or injury will turn out

look.title: Then and Now
look.text: An Egyptian healer feels a patient's broken jaw and decides it can be treated. Today a doctor looks at an X-ray of a broken wrist and says it should heal in about six weeks with a cast.
look.prompt: What step do both healers take before they begin treatment? Name it with a word from this lesson.

check.q: What is a prognosis?
choices: A prediction about how an illness will turn out
A prayer to a healing god
check.why: A prognosis is a prediction about the likely outcome of an illness or injury.

check.q: Which Greek writer praised Egyptian doctors?
check.why: Herodotus, about 440 BCE, wrote that Egyptian healers each focused on one part of the body.

check.q: Which habit from the Edwin Smith cases do modern doctors share?
choices: Examining the patient before choosing care
Treating every injury the same way
check.why: The cases ask the healer to examine first and decide second, as doctors do today.

sections.title: Greek Medicine and the Four Humors

lessons.title: Temples of Asclepius
lessons.mainIdea: Many ancient Greeks sought healing at temples of the god Asclepius, where they slept and hoped for a helpful dream.
reading: In ancient Greece, sick people often traveled to a temple of *Asclepius*. The Greeks honored Asclepius as the god of healing. One of his most famous temples was at Epidaurus, in southern Greece. Visitors bathed, made offerings and prayed there.

Then came *incubation*. In this practice, a patient slept in a special hall of the temple. Greeks believed the god might appear in a dream and show a cure. Priests helped explain the dreams. Stone tablets at Epidaurus record thanks from people who said they were healed.

Historians see these temples as part of Greek religious life. Rest, clean water, calm and hope may have helped some visitors feel better. The staff with a snake wrapped around it, called the rod of Asclepius, is still a symbol of medicine today.

words.d: the ancient Greek god of healing
the Greek temple practice of sleeping in a sacred hall in hope of a healing dream

look.title: A Visit to Epidaurus
look.text: Picture a traveler walking up a quiet valley to Epidaurus. She bathes in spring water, leaves a small gift at the altar and lies down on a mat in a long stone hall. Around her, others sleep too. In the morning, a priest asks about her dreams.
look.prompt: List two parts of this visit that might help a person feel better, even without a miracle.

check.q: Who was Asclepius?
check.why: The Greeks honored Asclepius as the god of healing.

check.q: What happened during incubation at a temple of Asclepius?
choices: Patients slept and hoped for a healing dream
check.why: Incubation meant sleeping in a special hall in hope that the god would show a cure in a dream.

check.q: Which symbol from these temples is still used for medicine?
choices: A staff with one snake around it
check.why: The rod of Asclepius, a staff with a snake, is still a symbol of medicine.

lessons.title: Hippocrates of Kos
lessons.mainIdea: Hippocrates and his followers taught that illness has natural causes that healers can observe and study.
reading: Hippocrates lived on the Greek island of Kos, about 460 to 370 BCE. We know little about his life. Many writings carry his name, but historians think many authors wrote them over many years. Together they are called the *Hippocratic Corpus*. A corpus is a body of writings.

The big idea in these writings is that illness has *natural causes*. That means causes in the body or the world, like food, weather or water, not the anger of gods. One text, On the Sacred Disease, is about seizures. It argues that seizures come from the brain, not from the gods.

Hippocratic doctors watched patients over days and wrote notes. They paid attention to diet, sleep and exercise. The Hippocratic Oath asked doctors to help the sick and do no harm on purpose. Doctors today still take oaths inspired by it, though the words have changed.

words.d: a large group of ancient Greek medical writings linked to Hippocrates and his followers
causes found in the body or the world, not in magic or the anger of gods

look.title: On the Sacred Disease
look.text: This illness is no more divine or sacred than other diseases. It has a natural cause, just as other illnesses do. People call it divine only because they do not understand it.
look.cite: Hippocratic Corpus, On the Sacred Disease, about 400 BCE
look.prompt: What does the writer say is the real reason people called this illness sacred?

check.q: What is the Hippocratic Corpus?
choices: A group of Greek medical writings by many authors
check.why: The Hippocratic Corpus is a body of medical writings by Hippocrates and many followers.

check.q: According to On the Sacred Disease, where do seizures come from?
check.why: The text argues seizures come from the brain and have a natural cause.

check.q: What did the Hippocratic Oath ask doctors to do?
choices: Help the sick and not harm them on purpose
check.why: The Oath asked doctors to help the sick and do no harm on purpose.

lessons.title: The Four Humors
lessons.mainIdea: Greek medicine taught that health came from a balance of four body fluids called humors.
reading: Hippocratic writers had a theory about the body. A *theory* is an idea that tries to explain many things at once. They said the body holds four fluids, called the four *humors*. The humors were blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile.

In this theory, health meant the humors were in balance. Illness meant one humor was too strong or too weak. A cold with a runny nose seemed to show too much phlegm. Fever and a red face seemed to show too much blood. Healers linked each humor to a season as well.

To bring back *balance*, healers changed a patient's diet, rest and exercise. They also used bloodletting, which means removing some blood on purpose. The humors theory made sense to people because it was based on things they could see, like mucus and fever. It shaped medicine for about 2,000 years.

words.d: the four body fluids in the old Greek theory: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile
an idea that tries to explain many observations at once
in humors theory, the healthy state where no fluid is too strong or too weak

look.title: Explaining a Cold
look.text: A patient in ancient Athens has a runny nose, a cough and feels chilly. It is winter. A Hippocratic doctor says there is too much phlegm, a cold and wet humor, and tells the patient to eat warm, dry foods and rest.
look.prompt: What did the doctor observe correctly? What explanation did the doctor get wrong, based on what we know today?

check.q: Which list names the four humors?
choices: Blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile
check.why: The four humors were blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile.

check.q: In humors theory, what caused illness?
choices: Bad luck from the stars only
check.why: The theory said illness came when one humor was too strong or too weak.

check.q: What was bloodletting?
choices: Removing some blood on purpose to restore balance
check.why: Healers used bloodletting, removing blood on purpose, to try to restore balance.

lessons.title: Why the Humors Were Replaced
lessons.mainIdea: New evidence about cells and germs in the 1800s showed the humors theory was wrong, so doctors set it aside.
reading: The humors theory lasted a very long time. Doctors in Europe and the Middle East used it into the 1800s. Bloodletting was still common in the early 1800s. Many patients were weakened by it, because losing blood makes it harder to fight illness.

Science slowly tested the theory. In 1858 the German doctor Rudolf Virchow argued that disease starts in the body's *cells*, the tiny living units that make up the body. In the 1860s to 1880s, Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch showed that many diseases are caused by *germs*, tiny living things such as bacteria.

Doctors could now see causes under the microscope and test treatments. The four humors did not match this evidence, so the theory was set aside. This is how science works. A popular idea can last for centuries, but it changes when careful tests show something better.

words.d: the tiny living units that make up every part of the body
tiny living things, such as bacteria, that can cause disease

look.title: How Long Some Medical Ideas Lasted
look.cite: Rounded spans from standard histories, e.g. Roy Porter, The Greatest Benefit to Mankind, 1997
look.prompt: The humors theory lasted much longer than germ theory so far. Does lasting a long time prove an idea is right? Explain.

check.q: Who argued in 1858 that disease starts in the body's cells?
check.why: Rudolf Virchow argued in 1858 that disease starts in cells.

check.q: What did Pasteur and Koch show?
choices: That the four humors were correct
That many diseases are caused by germs
check.why: Pasteur and Koch showed that germs such as bacteria cause many diseases.

check.q: Why was the humors theory finally set aside?
choices: It did not match new evidence about cells and germs
check.why: Tests and microscopes showed causes that the humors theory could not explain.

lessons.title: Galen of Pergamon
lessons.mainIdea: Galen, a Greek doctor in the Roman Empire in the 100s CE, studied anatomy through animal dissection and wrote many books.
reading: Galen was born about 129 CE in Pergamon, a Greek city in what is now Turkey. As a young doctor, he treated gladiators in Pergamon. Their wounds let him see muscles and organs up close. Later he moved to Rome and became a doctor to emperors.

Galen studied *anatomy*, the structure of the body. Human dissection was not allowed in Rome. So he did *dissection* on animals such as pigs and monkeys. Dissection means carefully cutting open a body to study its parts. In one famous test, he showed that arteries carry blood, not air, as some earlier doctors thought.

Galen wrote a huge number of books. He accepted the four humors and built on them. He also did experiments, like tying off nerves in animals to see what stopped working. That was a real step toward testing ideas instead of only arguing about them.

words.d: the study of the structure and parts of the body
carefully cutting open a body to study its parts

look.title: Galen on Seeing for Yourself
look.text: Anyone who wishes to see the works of nature should trust their own eyes, not books about anatomy alone. Look carefully at the body itself.
look.cite: Galen, On Anatomical Procedures, 2nd century CE, general sense of his advice
look.prompt: Galen tells readers to trust their own eyes. Why is it surprising that later doctors trusted Galen's books over their own eyes?

check.q: Where was Galen born?
check.why: Galen was born about 129 CE in Pergamon, in what is now Turkey.

check.q: Why did Galen dissect animals instead of humans?
choices: Human dissection was not allowed in Rome
check.why: Human dissection was not allowed, so he dissected pigs and monkeys.

check.q: What did Galen show about arteries?
check.why: Galen showed that arteries carry blood, not air.

lessons.title: Galen's Long Shadow
lessons.mainIdea: Galen's books guided doctors for over 1,300 years, until Andreas Vesalius corrected many of his mistakes in 1543.
reading: After Galen died, about 216 CE, his books spread widely. Scholars in the Islamic world translated them into Arabic and added their own ideas. Later they were translated into Latin for European universities. For centuries, doctors learned anatomy mainly from Galen's writings, which gave him great *authority*.

But Galen had studied animals, not people. Some parts of animal bodies are different from human bodies. For example, he described a jawbone in two pieces and a liver with many lobes, as in some animals. Because of his authority, few people questioned these errors.

In 1543 the anatomist Andreas Vesalius published On the Fabric of the Human Body. He had dissected human bodies himself in Padua, Italy. His careful drawings corrected many of Galen's mistakes. Vesalius still respected Galen, but he trusted *evidence* he could see over old books.

words.d: the power to be trusted or believed, often because of reputation
facts or observations that show whether an idea is true

look.title: Book or Body?
look.text: A student in 1540 opens Galen's book. It says the human jawbone has two parts. On the table in front of him is a human skull. The jawbone is clearly one piece.
look.prompt: What should the student trust, and why? What might make it hard for him to say so out loud?

check.q: Who corrected many of Galen's anatomy mistakes in 1543?
check.why: Vesalius published On the Fabric of the Human Body in 1543 and corrected many errors.

check.q: Why did Galen make some anatomy mistakes?
choices: He studied animal bodies, which differ from human bodies
check.why: Galen dissected animals, and some animal parts differ from human parts.

check.q: How did Galen's books reach later European universities?
choices: They were carved on temple walls
Through Arabic translations and later Latin ones
check.why: Scholars translated Galen into Arabic, and later his work was translated into Latin.

lessons.title: Water, Baths and Public Health
lessons.mainIdea: Rome built aqueducts, baths and sewers that brought clean water to many people and carried waste away.
reading: Ancient Rome was a crowded city, with perhaps a million people at its peak. Crowded cities need clean water. In 312 BCE the Romans built the Aqua Appia, their first *aqueduct*. An aqueduct is a channel that carries water from far away, often using a gentle downhill slope.

Over the next centuries Rome built about eleven major aqueducts. The water flowed to public fountains, homes of the rich and large public *baths*. Many Romans visited the baths almost daily to wash, exercise and meet friends. A great drain called the Cloaca Maxima carried waste water toward the Tiber River.

These projects are early examples of *public health*, which means protecting the health of a whole community. The Romans did not know about germs. Still, clean water and drains help stop the spread of many diseases. Around 97 CE, the official Frontinus wrote a book about managing Rome's water.

words.d: a channel or bridge that carries water from a distant source to a city
work that protects the health of a whole community, such as clean water
large Roman public buildings for washing, exercise and meeting friends

look.title: Frontinus Brags About the Aqueducts
look.text: Compare these many great structures that carry so much water with the useless pyramids or the famous but idle works of the Greeks.
look.cite: Sextus Julius Frontinus, On the Water Supply of the City of Rome, about 97 CE
look.prompt: Why does Frontinus think aqueducts are better than pyramids? Do you agree?

check.q: What was the Aqua Appia?
check.why: The Aqua Appia, built in 312 BCE, was Rome's first aqueduct.

check.q: What is public health?
choices: Protecting the health of a whole community
Treating one patient in a temple
check.why: Public health means protecting a whole community, as clean water and drains do.

check.q: What did the Cloaca Maxima do?
choices: It brought drinking water to Rome
It carried waste water toward the Tiber River
It was a hospital for gladiators
check.why: The Cloaca Maxima was a great drain that carried waste water toward the Tiber.

review.q: Which Egyptian roll describes 48 injury cases from the head downward?
choices: On the Fabric of the Human Body
review.why: The Edwin Smith Papyrus describes 48 cases starting at the head.

review.q: How did Hippocratic writers explain illness differently from temple healing?
choices: They looked for natural causes in the body and world
review.why: Hippocratic writers taught that illness has natural causes, not divine ones.

review.q: Which fluid was NOT one of the four humors?
review.why: The four humors were blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. Lymph was not one.

review.q: Why did Galen's mistakes last so long?
choices: Vesalius agreed with all of them
His books had great authority and few people questioned them
review.why: Galen's authority was so great that few questioned his errors until Vesalius.

review.q: What evidence helped replace the humors theory?
choices: Discoveries about cells and germs in the 1800s
review.why: Virchow's work on cells and Pasteur and Koch's work on germs did not fit the humors.

review.q: Which Roman project best shows public health?
choices: Aqueducts bringing clean water to the city
review.why: Aqueducts helped a whole community by bringing clean water.

review.q: What does the rod of Asclepius stand for today?
review.why: The staff with a snake, linked to the Greek healing god, is a symbol of medicine.

review.q: What habit links the Edwin Smith Papyrus, Hippocrates and Vesalius?
review.why: Each looked closely at patients or bodies and recorded what they saw.
